where: Section 3, the sentence justifying the addition rule
problem: It says adding counts works 'because the probabilities multiply: e^−λ₁ e^−λ₂ = e^−(λ₁+λ₂)'. That product is only P(X=0 and Y=0), i.e. the k=0 case. For general k, P(X+Y=k) = Σ P(X=i)P(Y=k−i), not P(X=k)P(Y=k). As written, a student will conclude the sum distribution is found by multiplying individual probabilities, which is false.
fix: The addition rule follows from the convolution: P(X+Y=k) = Σ_{i=0}^{k} e^−λ₁ λ₁^i/i! · e^−λ₂ λ₂^(k−i)/(k−i)! = e^−(λ₁+λ₂)(λ₁+λ₂)^k/k!, using the binomial theorem. The product e^−λ₁ e^−λ₂ = e^−(λ₁+λ₂) is only the k = 0 case (no events in either count).

problem: 'The binomial coefficient factor tends to 1/k!' is loosely worded: C(n,k) itself grows without limit, so a student may write C(n,k) → 1/k! in an exam and lose marks. It is the combination C(n,k)p^k that tends to λ^k/k!.
fix: Write p = λ/n. Then C(n,k)p^k = [n(n−1)...(n−k+1)/n^k]·λ^k/k! → λ^k/k!, since the bracket tends to 1. Also (1−λ/n)^n → e^−λ and (1−λ/n)^(−k) → 1. Multiplying gives e^−λ λ^k/k!.
